q: The basic idea of VSEPR theory is that the electron pairs in the valence shell of a central atom:
o: Attract one another and crowd together on one side
Repel one another and stay as far apart as possible
Are all shared equally with the surrounding atoms
Move into the inner shells of the central atom
x: Bond pairs and lone pairs around the central atom repel each other, so they take up positions as far apart as possible. That arrangement decides the shape of the molecule.

q: Silane, SiH₄, has four bond pairs and no lone pair around silicon. The H–Si–H bond angle is about:
x: Four bond pairs with no lone pair arrange themselves tetrahedrally, giving 109.5°. 107° would need one lone pair, as in NH₃.

q: Which of the following molecules is linear?
x: In CS₂ the carbon has two double-bond regions and no lone pair, so they lie at 180°. H₂S, SO₂ and OF₂ all have lone pairs on the central atom and are bent.

q: A lone pair repels more strongly than a bond pair because a lone pair:
o: Contains more electrons than a bond pair
Is held by only one nucleus and so spreads out more
Lies farther from the central nucleus
x: A lone pair is attracted by only the central nucleus, so its electron cloud is broader and closer to the central atom, pushing bond pairs together. Both lone and bond pairs contain two electrons.

q: The H–N–H bond angle in NH₄⁺ (109.5°) is larger than in NH₃ (107°) because in NH₄⁺:
o: Nitrogen has two lone pairs instead of one
The lone pair of nitrogen has become a bond pair
x: When NH₃ accepts H⁺, its lone pair forms the fourth N–H bond. Four equal bond pairs give a regular tetrahedron of 109.5°, with no extra lone-pair repulsion.

q: In which of the following species are all the bond angles equal to 120°?
x: The carbonate ion has three bonding regions and no lone pair on carbon, so it is trigonal planar with 120° angles. PCl₅ has both 120° and 90° angles; NH₃ and H₃O⁺ are pyramidal.

q: When VSEPR theory is applied to CO₂, each C=O double bond is treated as:
o: Two separate bond pairs pointing in different directions
A lone pair on the carbon atom
One bonding region, like a single bond
x: For predicting shape, a double or triple bond counts as one region of electron density. Carbon in CO₂ therefore has two regions, which lie at 180°.

q: Water has a bond angle of 104.5°. When a water molecule accepts a proton to become H₃O⁺, its bond angle:
o: Decreases, because oxygen now has more bond pairs
Stays the same, because both are based on four electron pairs
Increases to 120°, because H₃O⁺ becomes trigonal planar
Increases, because oxygen now has one lone pair instead of two
x: In H₃O⁺ one lone pair of oxygen is used to bond H⁺, leaving one lone pair (pyramidal, about 107°). Water has two lone pairs, which squeeze the angle to 104.5°.

q: Between two atoms, a pi (π) bond can form only when:
o: The atoms are of the same element
The atoms use s orbitals for bonding
A sigma bond is already present between them
No sigma bond is present between them
x: A π bond never exists alone; the first bond between two atoms is always a σ bond, and π bonds are added in double and triple bonds.

q: How many sigma (σ) and pi (π) bonds are present in hydrogen cyanide, H–C≡N?
x: The C–H single bond is one σ bond. The C≡N triple bond has one σ and two π bonds. Total: 2 σ and 2 π.

q: In a sigma (σ) bond, the electron density is:
o: Present only above and below the line joining the nuclei
Located only on the more electronegative atom
Concentrated along the line joining the two nuclei
Spread evenly over the whole molecule
x: A σ bond forms by head-on overlap, so electron density lies along the internuclear axis and is symmetrical around it. Density above and below the axis describes a π bond.

q: The bond in a hydrogen molecule, H₂, is formed by:
o: Overlap of two 1s orbitals, giving a pi bond
Overlap of two 1s orbitals, giving a sigma bond
Overlap of a 1s and a 2p orbital
x: Each hydrogen atom has only a 1s orbital. Two s orbitals can only overlap head-on, so the bond is a σ (s–s) bond.

q: The H–Cl bond in hydrogen chloride is:
o: A pi bond formed by overlap of an s and a p orbital
A sigma bond formed by overlap of two s orbitals
A sigma bond formed by overlap of an s and a p orbital
A pi bond formed by sideways overlap of two p orbitals
x: The 1s orbital of hydrogen overlaps head-on with a half-filled 3p orbital of chlorine, giving an s–p σ bond.

q: Ethanoic acid (acetic acid), CH₃COOH, contains how many σ and π bonds in total?
x: σ bonds: three C–H, one C–C, one in C=O, one C–O and one O–H = 7. Only the C=O double bond has a π bond, so there is 1 π.

q: The nitrogen molecule, N≡N, contains:
o: Two sigma and one pi bond
One sigma and two pi bonds
x: A triple bond is made of one σ bond (head-on overlap) and two π bonds (sideways overlap of two pairs of p orbitals).

q: The two CH₃ groups in ethane can rotate freely about the C–C bond because:
o: The overlap of a sigma bond is symmetrical about the bond axis
The C–C bond contains a pi bond
The carbon atoms are sp² hybridised
Ethane has lone pairs on each carbon atom
x: A σ bond is cylindrically symmetrical, so rotating one end does not reduce the overlap. A π bond would be broken by rotation, which is why C=C bonds do not rotate freely.

q: The hybridisation of the carbon atom in carbon dioxide, O=C=O, is:
x: Carbon forms two σ bonds and has no lone pair, so it uses two sp hybrid orbitals at 180°. Its two remaining p orbitals form the two π bonds.

q: When one s orbital mixes with three p orbitals, the number of hybrid orbitals formed is:
x: The number of hybrid orbitals always equals the number of atomic orbitals mixed: 1 s + 3 p gives four sp³ hybrid orbitals.

q: The electronegativity of a carbon atom increases with the s character of its hybrid orbitals. Which order of electronegativity is correct?
o: sp³ carbon > sp² carbon > sp carbon
sp carbon > sp² carbon > sp³ carbon
sp² carbon > sp carbon > sp³ carbon
x: s character is 50% in sp, 33% in sp² and 25% in sp³. More s character holds electrons closer to the nucleus, so sp carbon is the most electronegative.

q: The hybridisation of the carbon atom in methanal (formaldehyde), HCHO, is:
x: Carbon forms three σ bonds (two C–H, one C–O) and one π bond with oxygen, so it uses three sp² hybrid orbitals and one unhybridised p orbital.

q: In the ammonium ion, NH₄⁺, the nitrogen atom is:
x: Nitrogen has four σ bond pairs and no lone pair in NH₄⁺, so it uses four sp³ hybrid orbitals arranged tetrahedrally.

q: Which molecule contains carbon atoms with all three types of hybridisation, sp³, sp² and sp?
x: In CH₃–CH=CH–C≡CH the CH₃ carbon is sp³, the two C=C carbons are sp² and the two C≡C carbons are sp. Each of the other molecules lacks one of these types.

q: In ethyne, HC≡CH, how many unhybridised p orbitals does each carbon atom have?
x: Each carbon is sp hybridised, using one s and one p orbital. The other two p orbitals stay unhybridised and form the two π bonds of the triple bond.

q: How many sp³-hybridised carbon atoms are present in pent-1-ene, CH₂=CHCH₂CH₂CH₃?
x: The two carbons of the C=C bond are sp². The remaining three carbons (CH₂, CH₂ and CH₃) form only single bonds, so they are sp³.

q: In tetrachloromethane, CCl₄, carbon has four bond pairs and no lone pair. The shape of CCl₄ is:
x: Four bond pairs with no lone pair get as far apart as possible in a tetrahedral arrangement, with angles of 109.5°.

q: In PF₅, phosphorus has five bond pairs and no lone pair. The shape of the molecule is:
x: Five bond pairs give a trigonal bipyramid: three equatorial bonds at 120° and two axial bonds at 90° to them. Six bond pairs would give an octahedron.

q: In gaseous mercury(II) chloride, HgCl₂, mercury has two bond pairs and no lone pair. The shape of the molecule is:
x: Two bond pairs with no lone pair repel each other to opposite sides, giving a linear molecule with a 180° angle. A bent shape needs lone pairs on the central atom.

q: What is the shape of oxygen difluoride, OF₂, in which oxygen carries two lone pairs besides its two O–F bonds?
x: Four electron pairs are arranged roughly tetrahedrally, but only two are bonds, so the molecule is bent like water.

q: A molecule AB₂ is bent with a bond angle of about 104.5°. How many lone pairs are on the central atom A?
x: Four electron pairs (two bonding, two lone) give the bent shape with an angle near 104.5°, as in water. With no lone pair AB₂ would be linear.

q: A molecule XY₃ is found to be trigonal planar. What can be concluded about the central atom X?
o: It has three bond pairs and one lone pair
It has three bond pairs and no lone pair
It has two bond pairs and one lone pair
It has four bond pairs and no lone pair
x: Three bond pairs alone spread out at 120° in a plane. A lone pair as well would push the bonds down into a pyramid, as in NH₃.

q: SO₂ and H₂O are both bent molecules. Which statement about them is correct?
o: Both central atoms have two lone pairs, so their bond angles are equal
Sulphur in SO₂ has two lone pairs, so its angle is smaller than in water
Neither central atom has a lone pair; they are bent because of their double bonds
Sulphur in SO₂ has one lone pair, while oxygen in H₂O has two, so the angle in water is smaller
x: In SO₂ sulphur has two bonding regions and one lone pair (angle close to 120°). In H₂O oxygen has two lone pairs, which squeeze the angle to 104.5°.

q: Which of these molecules has a net dipole moment?
x: CHCl₃ is tetrahedral but has one C–H bond and three C–Cl bonds, so the bond dipoles do not cancel. The other three are symmetrical and non-polar.

q: CCl₄ is non-polar but CHCl₃ is polar. The reason is that in CHCl₃:
o: The molecule is planar instead of tetrahedral
The carbon atom has a lone pair
Replacing one Cl by H makes the bond dipoles unequal, so they no longer cancel
x: Both are tetrahedral. In CCl₄ four identical C–Cl dipoles cancel; in CHCl₃ the C–H dipole is different from the C–Cl dipoles, leaving a net dipole moment.

q: Which isomer of 1,2-dichloroethene has zero dipole moment?
o: The cis isomer, because the two Cl atoms are on the same side
Both isomers, because they have the same atoms
Neither isomer, because C–Cl bonds are always polar
The trans isomer, because the two C–Cl dipoles point in opposite directions
x: In the trans isomer the two C–Cl bond dipoles are opposite and cancel. In the cis isomer they point to the same side, giving a net dipole moment.

q: SO₂ has a dipole moment but SO₃ does not. This is because:
o: S–O bonds in SO₃ are non-polar
SO₂ is bent, while SO₃ is trigonal planar and symmetrical
SO₂ is linear, while SO₃ is pyramidal
Sulphur is more electronegative than oxygen in SO₃
x: In planar SO₃ the three S–O dipoles at 120° cancel. In bent SO₂ the two S–O dipoles add up to a net dipole.

q: Which statement about a molecule that contains polar bonds is correct?
o: It is non-polar only if it contains a lone pair
It is polar only if it is linear
It may still be non-polar if its shape makes the bond dipoles cancel
x: Polarity of a molecule depends on bond polarity and shape together. CO₂ and CCl₄ have polar bonds but are non-polar because their symmetrical shapes cancel the dipoles.

q: Of the three isomeric dichlorobenzenes, which one is non-polar?
x: In 1,4-dichlorobenzene the two C–Cl dipoles lie on opposite sides of the flat ring and cancel. In the 1,2 and 1,3 isomers the dipoles are at an angle and do not cancel.

q: Which molecule has polar bonds but is non-polar overall?
x: SiF₄ is tetrahedral with four identical Si–F dipoles that cancel. NF₃ is pyramidal and OF₂ is bent, so they are polar; HF has only one polar bond.

q: A covalent bond between two different atoms has some ionic character because:
o: Electrons are completely transferred from one atom to the other
The shared electron pair is pulled more towards the more electronegative atom
Both atoms have exactly the same electronegativity
The bond contains a lone pair
x: When the atoms differ in electronegativity, the shared pair lies closer to one atom, which gets a partial negative charge. Complete transfer would make the bond fully ionic.

q: The observed dipole moment of HBr is 0.80 D. The dipole moment calculated for HBr as a 100% ionic compound is 5.0 D. The percentage ionic character of the H–Br bond is:
x: % ionic character = (0.80 / 5.0) × 100 = 16%. 84% is the covalent part, and 62.5% comes from dividing the wrong way round.

q: Two atoms with electronegativities 3.0 and 0.9 form a bond. The electronegativity difference shows that the bond is:
o: A polar covalent bond with little ionic character
x: The difference is 2.1, which is greater than about 1.7, the value that corresponds to roughly 50% ionic character. So the bond is mainly ionic.

q: Electronegativities: C 2.5, H 2.1. The C–H bond is best described as:
o: Highly polar, with H as the negative end
x: An electronegativity difference of only 0.4 gives very little charge separation, so the C–H bond is nearly non-polar. This is why hydrocarbons are non-polar.

q: The C–Cl bond is polar, but the Cl–Cl bond is not. The reason is that:
o: The C–Cl bond is a double bond
Carbon is more electronegative than chlorine
Chlorine is more electronegative than carbon, while the two atoms in Cl₂ are identical
x: In Cl–Cl both atoms attract the shared pair equally, so there is no ionic character. In C–Cl the more electronegative chlorine pulls the pair towards itself.

q: To find the percentage ionic character of a bond, its observed dipole moment is compared with:
o: The dipole moment of the H–H bond
The dipole moment calculated assuming complete transfer of an electron
The bond energy of the same bond
x: % ionic character = (observed μ ÷ μ for a fully ionic bond) × 100, where the fully ionic value assumes a whole electronic charge at each end of the bond.

q: A bond has 20% ionic character. If it were 100% ionic, its dipole moment would be 5.5 D. Its observed dipole moment is:
x: Observed μ = 20% of 5.5 D = 0.20 × 5.5 = 1.1 D. 4.4 D is the 80% remainder, and 27.5 D comes from dividing by 0.20.

q: The rule "like dissolves like" means that:
o: Ionic solutes dissolve only in non-polar solvents
Polar solutes dissolve in polar solvents, and non-polar solutes in non-polar solvents
A solute dissolves only in a solvent of the same molar mass
x: Substances with similar intermolecular forces mix well. Polar or ionic substances dissolve in polar solvents like water; non-polar ones dissolve in solvents like benzene or hexane.

q: Non-polar covalent substances such as methane and tetrachloromethane have low melting and boiling points because:
o: Their covalent bonds are very weak
Only weak forces act between their molecules
They contain ions held by strong forces
x: Melting and boiling separate molecules, not break covalent bonds. Between non-polar molecules there are only weak intermolecular forces, so little energy is needed.

q: Fluoromethane, CH₃F (M = 34), boils at a higher temperature than ethane, C₂H₆ (M = 30). The main reason is that:
o: CH₃F has a much larger molar mass
CH₃F is polar, so dipole–dipole forces act between its molecules
The C–F bond is broken during boiling
x: The molar masses are similar, so the difference comes from polarity. The polar C–F bond gives CH₃F a dipole, adding dipole–dipole attraction that ethane lacks.

q: Dry hydrogen chloride gas does not conduct electricity, but its solution in water does. This is because HCl:
o: Is a polar molecule that ionises in water into H₃O⁺ and Cl⁻ ions
Is an ionic compound in the gas state
Becomes non-polar when dissolved in water
Reacts with water to form chlorine gas
x: HCl is a polar covalent molecule. Polar water molecules pull it apart into ions, and the ions carry the current.

q: Which liquid mixes completely with water?
x: Propanone is polar (C=O group) and forms hydrogen bonds with water through its oxygen, so it mixes in all proportions. The other three are non-polar.

q: Grease stains on cloth are removed with petrol rather than with water because:
o: Grease is ionic and dissolves only in petrol
Grease is non-polar and dissolves in non-polar petrol
Water is non-polar and cannot dissolve grease
Petrol reacts chemically with grease to form salts
x: Grease and petrol are both non-polar hydrocarbons, so grease dissolves in petrol. Water is polar and does not dissolve non-polar grease.

q: Sodium chloride melts at 801 °C, but hydrogen chloride is a gas at room temperature. The best explanation is that:
o: The H–Cl covalent bond is weaker than the attractions in NaCl
NaCl has a lattice of ions held by strong electrostatic forces, while HCl has separate molecules held by weak intermolecular forces
Chlorine is more electronegative in NaCl than in HCl
x: Melting NaCl means breaking the strong forces between all the ions. Boiling HCl only separates polar molecules held by weak dipole forces; the H–Cl bond itself is not broken.

q: Bond energies are usually given in the unit:
x: Bond energy is the energy per mole of bonds, so it is expressed in kilojoules per mole. The debye is the unit of dipole moment.

q: Which molecule has the strongest bond between its two atoms?
x: N₂ has a triple bond (one σ, two π), O₂ a double bond, and F₂ and Cl₂ only single bonds. More bonds between the same pair of atoms means a higher bond energy.

q: Bond energies (kJ mol⁻¹): N≡N 945, H–H 436, N–H 391. What is ΔH for N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) → 2NH₃(g)?
x: Bonds broken: 945 + 3(436) = 2253 kJ. Bonds formed: 6 N–H = 6(391) = 2346 kJ. ΔH = 2253 − 2346 = −93 kJ.

q: Breaking all the bonds in one mole of water vapour, H₂O(g) → 2H(g) + O(g), needs 926 kJ. The average O–H bond energy is:
x: Each water molecule has two O–H bonds, so the average O–H bond energy = 926 ÷ 2 = 463 kJ mol⁻¹.

q: Which order of carbon–halogen bond energies is correct?
x: As the halogen atom gets larger from F to I, the bond gets longer and the overlap poorer, so bond energy decreases from C–F to C–I.

q: The C–H bond energy quoted in tables (about 414 kJ mol⁻¹) is called an average bond energy because:
o: All C–H bonds in every compound have exactly this energy
It is measured only for liquid compounds
It includes the energy needed to melt the compound
The energy needed to break each successive C–H bond in CH₄ is slightly different
x: Removing the first, second, third and fourth H from CH₄ needs different amounts of energy. The table value is the mean, and it also varies a little from compound to compound.

q: The bond energy of H–Cl is 431 kJ mol⁻¹ and that of H–I is 299 kJ mol⁻¹. Which conclusion is correct?
o: HCl is less stable to heat than HI
The H–I bond is shorter than the H–Cl bond
HI decomposes into its elements on heating more easily than HCl
x: A lower bond energy means the bond breaks more easily, so HI is less thermally stable. The weaker H–I bond is also longer, because iodine is a larger atom.
